title: Micromechanisms of split crack formation in aluminum alloy 5083-O plate under cryogenic temperatures
abstract: Abstract Hot-rolled 5083-O aluminum alloy has emerged as a strong candidate for use in storage tanks for liquefied hydrogen (LH₂) marine transport, owing to its performance under extreme cryogenic conditions. This study aims to investigate the micromechanisms and critical conditions for the formation of split cracks in 5083-O aluminum alloy at cryogenic temperatures. Tensile tests on smooth and notched round bar specimens and L–T direction C(T) tests were conducted at 293 K, 223 K, 123 K, and 4 K, while an S–L direction C(T) test was performed at 77 K. The fracture locus at each temperature was obtained by combining the results of notched round bar tests with finite element (FE) analyses. The results showed that the fracture locus of 5083-O is temperature-independent. Among the round bar specimens, split cracks were observed only in those tested at 4 K and in the R1 notched specimen at 123 K. For the C(T) specimens, split cracks occurred only in the 4 K tests. Furthermore, a three-stage model was established for the formation process of split cracks. To calibrate the model for 5083-O, FE analyses were conducted to determine the critical conditions for each stage at various temperatures. The results predicted by the developed model were compared with the C(T) test results at temperatures ranging from 123 to 293 K.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Hydrogen storage and transportation present major challenges for the widespread implementation of hydrogen energy systems [ 1 ], where maritime transportation of LH₂ is a critical link. However, the extremely low temperature of LH₂ (below 20 K), combined with increasing demands for larger storage capacities, imposes strict requirements on the cryogenic fracture resistance of candidate materials [ 2 ,  3 ]. To date, stainless steels [ 4 ,  5 ] and nickel-based alloys [ 6 ,  7 – 8 ] have been the primary materials considered for large-scale, above-ground LH₂ storage. In comparison, aluminum alloys offer a significant advantage in terms of low density, making them especially well-suited for LH₂ fuel tanks in maritime transport and aerospace applications. Hot-rolled Al-Mg alloy AA5083-O, which is already widely applied in liquefied natural gas (LNG) storage tanks operating at 111 K, is now being considered for use in large-scale LH₂ storage tanks for marine applications. Consequently, understanding its fracture behavior and resistance at even lower cryogenic temperatures is of critical importance.

To date, the fracture behavior of Al-Mg alloys has been widely investigated, with ductile fracture via micro-void coalescence identified as the dominant failure mechanism under ambient conditions [ 9 ]. However, brittle second phase in Al-Mg alloys could trigger intergranular fracture. Al 6 (Fe, Mn) is the most commonly observed second phase particles in Al-Mg alloys which weakens the grain boundary (GB) [ 10 ,  11 – 12 ]. Studies have indicated the effects of Al 6 (Fe, Mn) size on fracture mode [ 13 ,  14 ], where coarse Al 6 (Fe, Mn) particles were found harmful for mechanical properties [ 15 ], especially at cryogenic temperatures, as indicated by Son et al. [ 16 ]. Ma et al. [ 17 ] conducted fatigue tests on A5083-O and revealed an orientation-dependent growth rate of the crack, suggesting that α-Al(Mn,Fe)Si/Al 6 (Fe, Mn) phases at grain boundaries provide weak paths for crack growth.

Split cracks are a characteristic form of sub-cracking commonly observed in rolled materials; they are typically perpendicular to the primary crack, delaminating the material in thickness-direction. Existing research on split cracks in Al-Mg alloys is scarce. Nakayama and Takaai [ 18 ] observed the split cracks in Al-Mg alloys tested under low temperature Charpy impact tests. They indicated that the increase of second phase particles can cause split cracks. In addition to low-temperature Charpy impact tests [ 18 ,  19 ], split cracks in 5083 rolled plates were also reported in deep notched tensile tests [ 20 ]. Asano et al. [ 19 ] and Nakayama et al. [ 18 ] investigated the correlation between aging temperature and split-crack length in Charpy impact tests conducted at 77 K, ultimately attributing split-crack formation to grain boundary precipitation.

Compared to Al-Mg alloy plates, split cracks have been more frequently reported in cryogenic mechanical tests of Al-Li alloy plates [ 21 ,  22 – 23 ]. Study by Rao et al. [ 24 ] suggested the relationship between split crack formation and through-thickness stresses as well as recrystallization. Investigation by Tayon et al. [ 25 ] indicated the influence of lack of slip accommodation across the boundary on split cracks. Incremental polishing by Kalyanam et al. [ 26 ] revealed the shape of split cracks. Their further finite element method (FEM) study shows that the effect of split cracks on stress distribution is restrained in a small region.

Unlike in aluminum alloys, investigation on split cracks has been conducted for thermo-mechanical control-processed (TMCP) steel plates for decades. The causes of split-crack in TMCP steel plates were extensively studied [ 27 ,  28 ,  29 – 30 ]. Katsuta et al. [ 31 ,  32 ] demonstrated the toughening effect in TMCP steel plates. Due to the frequent occurrence of split cracks in TMCP steel, this phenomenon has come to be regarded as a functional advantage in practical applications.

Our previous research [ 33 ] observed that the split cracks in 5083-O aluminum alloy rolled plates at cryogenic temperatures originate from the microcracks in brittle Al₆(Fe, Mn) second phase particles. The microcracks subsequently penetrate the grain boundaries of the matrix and ultimately propagate to form split cracks. However, there remains a gap in the literature when it comes to modeling the critical conditions of these processes in aluminum alloys. In contrast, the modeling of similar processes in steel has been the subject of extensive research. For the cleavage mechanism involving microcracks initiated in cementite particles and propagating into the matrix, Petch modeled the process based on the Griffith criterion and incorporated the effect of grain size on the critical stress through the Hall–Petch relationship. Kawata et al. [ 34 ,  35 ] further extended the model by incorporating the effects of martensite–austenite constituents in bainitic microstructures and quantitatively accounting for the influence of slip line length and GB segregation. Yoshimura et al. [ 36 ] investigated the critical conditions for the intergranular fracture originated at cementite in tempered martensite. Shibanuma et al. [ 37 ,  38 ] divided the cleavage fracture process in ferritic steels into three stages: the initiation of microcracks within the ferrite, the penetration of these microcracks into the matrix, and the subsequent propagation of the cracks across grain boundaries into adjacent grains. Although such critical condition models have been studied to some extent in steels, the modeling of the split crack formation process in Al–Mg alloy plates remains unexplored.

In this study, the critical conditions governing split crack formation in 5083-O aluminum alloy under cryogenic temperatures were modeled and calibrated. Tensile tests using round bar specimens and L–T-oriented C(T) specimens were performed at 293 K, 223 K, 123 K, and 4 K, while an S–L-oriented C(T) test was conducted at 77 K. The fracture locus at each temperature was established by integrating notched round bar test results with finite element (FE) simulations. FE analyses were employed to identify the critical conditions corresponding to each stage of split crack formation across the various temperatures, and these conditions were subsequently modeled based on both experimental observations and numerical results.

sections.heading: Material and specimens
paragraphs:
The chemical compositions of the studied aluminum alloy 5083-O are presented in Table  1 . The plate was manufactured through hot rolling and annealing processes before being sectioned into specimens. The orientation notation used in this study follows the ASTM standard, where L denotes the rolling direction, T denotes the transverse direction, and S denotes the short transverse or thickness direction. The loading direction of the specimens was along the L direction. Due to the hot rolling process, the grains in the plate were elongated along the L direction and exhibited a tendency to form layers in the S direction, as shown in Fig.  1 . To minimize the microstructural inhomogeneity caused by rolling, all specimens were sectioned at either one-quarter or three-quarters of the plate thickness. The microstructure of hot-rolled 5083-O is shown in Fig.  2 . Pancake-shaped grains were observed. In the SL plane, Al 6 (Fe,Mn) formed at GB, as observed by our previous study [ 33 ].

sections.heading: Test
paragraphs:
Table  2  summarizes all of the tests tested at various temperatures and orientations, where L and S denote the loading direction of tensile tests, while L-T and S-L denote C(T) tests shown in Fig.  1 . Uniaxial tensile and C(T) tests were conducted at 293 K, 223 K, 123 K, and 4 K. The smooth and notched round bars were tested to fracture at loading rates of 0.5 mm/min and 0.15 mm/min, respectively. For the C(T) specimens, multiple interrupted tests were conducted at each temperature to obtain loading curves corresponding to different crack growth lengths. The loading type of C(T) test was Mode I with a loading speed of 0.5 mm/min. Load-line displacement was monitored by a clip gauge mounted on the specimen. After reaching the target displacement, unloading was performed. To enable accurate post-test crack length evaluation, cyclic loading was employed to generate a final fatigue fracture. All tests were performed on a Shimadzu EHF-EG100kN-20L testing system.

The test at 293 K was carried out directly in ambient air. For tests at 223 K, the specimens were cooled using an ethyl alcohol and dry ice mixture placed inside a chamber attached to the testing apparatus. A thermocouple positioned near the notch tip was used to track the specimen temperature, which was held at 223 K ± 2 K for more than 30 min before loading was exerted. For tests at 123 K, a nitrogen vapor spray system was employed. Specimens were placed in a cooling chamber and exposed to a stream of cold nitrogen gas, whose temperature was controlled by auxiliary heaters. A stable temperature of 123 K ± 2 K was maintained for no less than 30 min before mechanical loading began. For testing at 4 K and 77 K, specimens were cooled with liquid helium and liquid nitrogen, respectively, until they reached the target temperature. They remained immersed in the cooling medium for over 30 min before mechanical testing.

sections.heading: Results of round bar tensile tests
paragraphs: Figure  5  presents the load–displacement curves of the tensile tests of notched round bars at various temperatures. Noticeable load fluctuations are observed in the 4 K specimens. This is a phenomenon in which heat generated by plastic deformation causes the material to soften, resulting in a drop in load. As the load drops, heat generation also decreases, allowing the material to harden again [ 40 ]. Additionally, as the notch radius increases, the elongation of the 4 K specimens becomes progressively greater compared to those tested at higher temperatures. Fig. 5 Load–displacement curves of notched round bars:  a  R10;  b  R5;  c  R2;  d  R1

Figure  6  shows the fracture surfaces of the round bar specimens tested at temperatures ranging from 223 to 4 K. It can be observed that the occurrence of split cracks is influenced by both temperature and notch radius. No splits were observed in any of the specimens tested at 223 K. The specimens tested at 293 K, like those at 223 K, did not exhibit any split cracks and are therefore not presented. At 123 K, only the R1 specimen exhibited a small number of splits. In contrast, all notched round bar specimens tested at 4 K showed the presence of split cracks, with a general trend indicating that smaller notch radii resulted in a greater number of splits. sections.heading: Results of C(T) tests
paragraphs: This study focuses on the split phenomenon; therefore, the J–R curve results are not presented here. Those interested in this topic are referred to our previous study [ 33 ]. Figure  7 a–c show the fracture surfaces of C(T) specimens tested in the temperature range of 293 to 123 K. No apparent split cracks were observed on the primary fracture surfaces. Figure  7 d–f present the fracture surfaces of three specimens tested at 4 K, all of which exhibited split cracks. As shown in Fig.  7 d, split cracks had already formed at the early stage of primary crack extension, and their formation likely preceded that of the primary crack. In the C(T) test conducted in the S–L direction at 77 K, unstable crack propagation (pop-in phenomenon [ 41 ]) was observed during the growth of the main crack, as shown in Fig.  7 g and h. Further observations indicated that the fracture mode in the pop-in region is identical to the split crack formation mechanism observed in the L–T 4 K tests [ 33 ]. Fig. 7 Fracture surfaces of C(T) specimens:  a  293 K representative;  b  223 K representative;  c  123 K representative;  d  4 K No.1;  e  4 K No.2;  f  4 K No.3;  g  77 K;  h  load–displacement curve of 77 K S-L C(T) test

sections.heading: Stress–strain curve calibration
paragraphs: In the post-necking stage, piecewise linear extrapolation was employed to estimate the true stress–strain curve. A combined experimental–numerical approach was used to calibrate the stress–strain relationship in this stage. A two-dimensional axisymmetric FE model was constructed in Abaqus 2023 with the same dimensions as the smooth tensile specimen, as shown in Fig.  8 a. Displacement was applied at the far end to simulate the tensile process of the smooth round bar specimen, continuing until the gauge length (GL) displacement corresponding to the onset of fracture was reached. In each iteration, the estimated true stress–strain relationship was used to perform the FE analysis, where the isotropic yield criterion and the isotropic hardening model were applied. The resulting load–displacement curve from the FE simulation was compared with the experimental data, and the stress–strain curve was updated accordingly. This iterative process was repeated until the simulated load–displacement curve closely matched the experimental results. The final calibrated true stress–strain curves are shown in Fig.  8 b. Fig. 8 a  FE model for stress–strain curve calibration.  b  Calibrated true stress–strain curve

FE models for C(T) specimens
paragraphs: In the current study, FEM simulations without incorporating crack propagation were conducted to obtain critical stresses. The quarter-symmetric 3D model of the C(T) specimen is shown in Fig.  10 a, with a mesh size of 0.1 × 0.1 × 0.1 mm in the central region. The FEM simulation for the 77 K specimen aimed to obtain the stress distribution near the crack tip when pop-in occurred, while the simulation for the 4 K specimen focused on the stress distribution at the onset of damage at the primary crack tip. Therefore, different symmetric constraints were applied on the primary crack plane, as illustrated in Fig.  10 b. Symmetric boundary conditions in the thickness direction were applied over the entire cross section. In the FE analysis, the models were loaded under the same condition as in the experiment. Fig. 10 a  FE model for the C(T) specimen.  b  Symmetric displacement constraints for the two models, where the model for the 77 K specimen was intended to simulate the crack front shape at the onset of the pop-in of the primary crack, while the 4 K specimen model aimed to simulate the crack front shape at the initiation of the primary crack

Conclusion
paragraphs: In this study, a combined experimental and FEM approach was used to investigate the micromechanics and critical conditions for the formation of split cracks in 5083-O aluminum alloy in cryogenic fracture toughness tests. Tensile tests using smooth and notched round bar specimens, as well as C(T) tests in L–T direction, were conducted at 293 K, 223 K, 123 K, and 4 K. A C(T) test in S–L direction was conducted at 77 K.

Results from notched round bar tensile tests indicated a temperature-independent fracture locus. Among the round bar specimens, split cracks were observed only in the specimens tested at 4 K and in the R1 notched round bar specimen tested at 123 K. For the C(T) specimens, split cracks occurred only in the tests conducted at 4 K.
Finally, the developed model was validated through comparison with the numerical simulation results of crack propagation in C(T) tests.
